Loss of human life will occur from mining and reclamation operations and increased vehicular and train traffic. According to mining Enforcement and Safety Administration (MESA) statistics, the fatal accident rate at western surface coal mines in 1974 was .083 per million tons of coal produced. During the first nine months of 1975, the fatal and disabling accident rates in the strip mine industry were 0.41 and 9.24 per million man-hours. At the existing Westmoreland Resources surface mine on Tract III, approximately 6,000 man-hours are required to produce one million tons of coal. Disabling injuries and fatal accidents constitute an irretrievable commitment of human resources.
Topography and natural soil distribution and stratification will be irreversibly modified, as will the scenic character. The only ground-water aquifers that will be disrupted are those that will be physically removed during mining operations. Adjacent parts of these aquifers will be affected during mining operations. The chemical quality of water in the deeper aquifers will not be changed, but quality of water in the shallow aquifers in the area and down gradient could be irreversibly reduced. Seeps and springs in some locations may be permanently lost or altered. Approximately 26,000 acre feet of water drawn from the Madison formation for various uses will be irretrievably lost over the life of the project.
Losses of surface water by evaporation from sediment ponds are irretrievable.
